title: parseInt(0.0000005) returns 5, not 0
assumption: parseInt() reads the digits of the number you gave it, in the order you wrote them.

input.display: parseInt(0.0000005)  -- note: the NUMBER 0.0000005, not the string "0.0000005"
input.description: Calling parseInt on a small decimal number directly (rather than on a string), e.g. while sanitizing a computed fractional value into an integer.

what_goes_wrong: `parseInt(0.0000005)` returns 5 -- not 0, and not an error -- because the number gets stringified to scientific notation before parseInt ever sees a digit of the original decimal.
why: `parseInt` only accepts a string; when given a `number`, JavaScript first coerces it to a string via the Number-to-String algorithm. That algorithm switches to exponent notation for any magnitude below 1e-6 (and at or above 1e21), so 0.000001 stringifies as "0.000001" but 0.0000005 becomes "5e-7", not "0.0000005". `parseInt` then reads the string from the start, parsing digits until it hits the first character that isn't part of an integer -- which is "e" -- so it returns 5, the only digit it saw before stopping. Calling `parseInt("0.0000005")` on the literal string instead returns 0, because the string parse stops at the ".". The large end bites the same way: `parseInt(1e21)` is 1, because 1e21 stringifies as "1e+21".

repros.code:
console.log((0.0000005).toString());       // what parseInt actually sees
console.log(parseInt(0.0000005));           // number argument -> stringified first
console.log(parseInt("0.0000005"));         // string argument -> no scientific notation

repros.expected_output:
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '0.0000005'
0

fix: Never pass a `number` directly to `parseInt`; convert deliberately with `Math.trunc()`/`Math.floor()` for numbers, and reserve `parseInt` for strings whose format you've already validated.
